title: Mr. X & Coillte
text:
Decision
Mr. X & Coillte
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-160332-H2V7Y5
Published on 8 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether Coillte was justified in refusing the appellant’s request on the basis that no further environmental information within the scope of that request is held by or for it.
08 July 2026
Background
1. On 17 April 2025 the appellant made a request to Coillte under the AIE Regulations seeking access to the following information:
“Information that demonstrates that the use of fertilisers on sites where exotic coniferous species dominate is equally or more ecologically beneficial than the use of silvicultural systems that do not require fertilizers.”
2. On 16 May 2025, Coillte issued its original decision which refused access to the requested information in reliance of Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations, wherein the decision maker stated that “the information sought does not exist and therefore is not “held” by or for Coillte”.
3. The appellant sought an internal review of the decision on 19 May 2025.
4. Coillte issued its internal review decision on 18 June 2025, advising that following re-examination of the request that the decision made by the initial decision maker should be affirmed.
5. The appellant submitted an appeal to this Office on 04 July 2025.
6. I have now completed my review of this appeal under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and by Coillte. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
7. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
8. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
9. Pursuant to article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations, this review is concerned with whether Coillte was justified in refusing access to the information requested by the appellant on the basis that no further information within the scope of the request is held by Coillte.
Analysis and Findings
10. Article 7(1) of the AIE Regulations requires public authorities to make available environmental information that is held by or for them on request, subject only to the provisions of the AIE Regulations.
11. Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider, where the question arises as to whether the requested environmental information or any further environmental information is held by or for the public authority concerned. It provides as follows;
“Where a request is made to a public authority and the information requested is not held by or for the authority concerned, that authority shall inform the applicant as soon as possible that the information is not held by or for it”.
12. This Office’s approach to dealing with this type of case is to assess whether adequate steps have been taken to identify and locate relevant environmental information, having regard to the particular circumstances. In determining whether the steps taken are adequate in the circumstances, a standard of reasonableness is applied.
13. What will be considered reasonable will vary from case to case. Article 7(5) of the AIE regulations allows public authority to refuse a request if it does not hold the requested information. In order for a public authority to successfully rely on this provision, it must, among other things, provide evidence that it carried out adequate searches for the environmental information requested.
14. In its initial submission to this Office, Coillte detailed the searches undertaken, a summary of which I provide as follows:
• the AIE team consulted with two key subject matter experts (SMEs); the Establishment Process Manager, who is responsible for managing and coordinating Establishment operations across all Business Area Units (BAUs), including the application of fertilisers; and the Silvicultural Specialist, who provides technical support to the Establishment Process Manager and oversees various silvicultural research projects and trials aimed at improving forestry practices within Coillte. These discussions focused on whether such information is typically created or retained, and whether searches could be carried out to locate it.
• Coillte stated that the purpose of these searches consultations was twofold: i. to establish whether the type of information sought typically exists and/or is held by Coillte; and ii. to request that the SMEs undertake appropriate searches for any such information, if held.
• The authority further states that “SMEs were advised to conduct comprehensive searches across all relevant storage systems, including cloud-based platforms, Office 365/email systems, and team-based storage. These searches were carried out both electronically and physically, using a range of parameters such as file name, date, and keywords. The keywords/search terms employed included: ‘Exotic Conifer’, ‘Exotic Conifer Fertiliser’, and ‘Exotic Conifer Treatment’.”
• Based on these searches the authority stated that it was “satisfied that reasonable steps were taken to identify any relevant records, and it has been confirmed that no such information is held by or for Coillte”.
15. In relation to whether information relevant to the appellant’s request could be located elsewhere in the organisation Coillte submits that the “likelihood of such records being misfiled or stored outside the relevant business areas is extremely low”,
and “in the unlikely event that a record had been misfiled, it would still be identified through keyword searches conducted across our cloud-based storage systems”.
16. Within his statement of appeal, the appellant provided arguments as to why he believed that information on this subject should exist within Coillte. A summary of this submission is provided as follows:
• The appellant’s request is based on the conditions of the Irish FSC Interim National Standard which came into force on the 15th of July 2024.
• The appellant notes that as a result of information received from Coillte in a previous AIE request, the authority applied “over 1300 tonnes of fertiliser across its estate after the 15th of July 2024”.
• The appellant has provided further text to this Office where he contends that Coillte is a Forest Stewardship Council certificate holder and as such is bound by the standards of that body. One such standard highlighted by the appellant is as follows, “Criteria 10.6 The Organization* shall minimize or avoid the use of fertilizers*. When fertilizers* are used, The Organization* shall demonstrate that use is equally or more ecologically and economically beneficial than use of silvicultural* systems that do not require fertilizers, and prevent, mitigate, and/or repair damage to environmental values*, including soil”.
• As a result of the above the appellant contends that “my request is for information that Coillte would need to be able to evidence compliance to a third-party auditor. Therefore, records should exist. I appreciate that they may not exist, but this would involve a breach of certification standards. I therefore need to be clear that Coillte have taken all reasonable steps to identify the requested information”.
17. At the request of the investigator assigned to this appeal, Coillte provided additional clarification on a number of points which I summarise as follows:
• With regards to the possibility that information relevant to the appellants request may lie with third party contractors the authority states, “contractors are not involved in the design, management, or monitoring of fertiliser trials. Such trials are typically overseen by forestry researchers or relevant state bodies, and contractors would not be expected to hold or generate information relevant to the ecological assessment of fertiliser use in these contexts.”
• In relation to the search terms used the authority stated that both ‘fertiliser’ and ‘fertilizer’ were considered within the search terms as both spellings appear in the appellant’s request.
• Coillte has also confirmed that the silivicultural expert within the authority had returned no search results for the appellants request and the authority noted that the body had “not carried out any research projects or trials involving the non-use of fertiliser inputs and/or silviculture techniques in the establishment and maintenance of conifer plantations”.
• Coillte confirmed that “overall responsibility for fertiliser planning, use and reporting across the Coillte estate lies with the Establishment Process Manager”.
• With regards to the search terms used by the authority, the list initially provided by the authority was not exhaustive and other search terms used were “Exotic Conifer Fertilizer, Conifer Fertiliser / Conifer Fertilizer, Exotic Coniferous Fertiliser / Exotic Coniferous Fertilizer”.
18. In a separate submission to this Office, with regards to the possibility that information relevant to the appellants request may exist within a third party, the authority has further stated that Coillte “has not carried out any research projects or trials involving the non-use of fertiliser inputs and/or silvicultural techniques. Accordingly, there was no necessity to engage with forestry researchers and/or relevant state bodies in relation to such trials, as these have not been undertaken by Coillte.”
19. In order to provide the appellant with an opportunity to respond to the submissions of the authority a summary of these submissions was provide by the investigator in this appeal to which the appellant provided a lengthy response of which I intend to only provide the headings of as follows:
1. Coillte has still not demonstrated what searches were actually undertaken
2. The search terms remain conceptually too narrow
3. Coillte appears to have mischaracterised the request as being about “trials”
4. The focus on only two SMEs has not been justified
5. The response concerning contractors, researchers and state bodies is inadequate
6. The “misfiled records” reasoning is speculative and insufficient
7. There is a clear plausibility basis for expecting records to exist
8. The preliminary position should not be maintained
20. I note that the appellant has raised a number of queries in his appeal on the adequacies of searches carried out by the authority in question in response to his request. Having considered the search details provided, I am persuaded they satisfy what is required in the circumstances of this case. To be clear, article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations does not require a forensic trawling exercise to be conducted by public authorities, rather a test of reasonableness and an adequate search exercise should be performed. This Office does not generally expect public authorities to carry out extensive or indefinite general searches for records simply because an applicant asserts that more records should or might exist, or rejects a public authorises explanation of why a record does not exist.
21. The appellant has expressed concern that the search terms used by Coillte were too narrow. However, Coillte has explained that the keyword searches were not the only search method used. The searches were supplemented by consultation with the relevant subject-matter experts, including the officer with overall responsibility for fertiliser planning, use and reporting. Coillte also confirmed that both “fertiliser” and “fertilizer” were considered, and that broader terms such as “Conifer Fertiliser/Fertilizer” and “Exotic Coniferous Fertiliser/Fertilizer” were used. While it may be possible to identify additional search terms, article 7(5) does not require exhaustive or speculative searching. The question is whether the steps taken were reasonable in the circumstances.
22. Likewise, the appellant has, in his appeal, referred to the participation of the authority in a certification process which in his opinion places an onus on the authority to meet certain criteria of that scheme which may be of relevance to the subject matter of this appeal. The appellant’s position is that, by virtue of its participation in the FSC certification process, Coillte may be expected to demonstrate compliance with Criterion 10.6. However, my role in this appeal is not to determine whether Coillte has complied with FSC certification requirements, or whether records ought to have been created for that purpose. My role is confined to determining whether Coillte has taken reasonable and adequate steps to identify environmental information held by or for it within the scope of the appellant’s AIE request.
23. Having considered the submissions of both parties, I am satisfied that Coillte has taken reasonable and adequate steps to identify and locate information within the scope of the appellant’s request.
Decision
24. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I hereby affirm Coillte’s decision.
Appeal to the High Court
25. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Ger Deering
Commissioner for Environmental Information
